\]

---

### 1.  Square once  

Both sides are non‑negative, so we may square:

\[
5-\sqrt{5-x}=x^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\sqrt{5-x}=5-x^{2}.
\]

Since the square‑root is non‑negative we must have  

\[
5-x^{2}\ge0\ \Longrightarrow\ x\le\sqrt5 .
\tag{1}
\]

Also we need \(5-x\ge0\) (so that the inner root is defined), i.e. \(x\le5\).  
Thus the admissible interval is \(0<x\le\sqrt5\).

---

### 2.  Square again  

\[
5-x=(5-x^{2})^{2}.
\]

Expand the right‑hand side:

\[
5-x=x^{4}-10x^{2}+25 .
\]

Bring all terms to one side:

\[
x^{4}-10x^{2}+x+20=0.
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Factor the quartic  

The polynomial factors nicely:

\[
x^{4}-10x^{2}+x+20
=(x^{2}-x-4)(x^{2}+x-5).
\]

Thus (2) gives the four real roots

\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{2}-x-4=0 &\;\Longrightarrow\; 
x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{17}}{2},\\[2mm]
x^{2}+x-5=0 &\;\Longrightarrow\; 
x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{21}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 4.  Keep only the admissible solutions  

From (1) we need \(0<x\le\sqrt5\approx2.236\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{root} & \text{value} \\ \hline
\frac{1+\sqrt{17}}{2}\approx2.56 & >\sqrt5 \\
\frac{1-\sqrt{17}}{2}<0 & \text{reject}\\
\frac{-1-\sqrt{21}}{2}<0 & \text{reject}\\
\frac{-1+\sqrt{21}}{2}\approx1.79 & \text{ admissible}
\end{array}
\]

The only candidate that satisfies the domain restrictions is  

\[
x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{21}}{2}.
\]

---

### 5.  Verify it satisfies the original equation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5-x}}
&= \sqrt{5-\sqrt{5-\frac{-1+\sqrt{21}}{2}}}\\
&= \sqrt{5-\sqrt{\frac{9-\sqrt{21}}{2}}}
= \frac{-1+\sqrt{21}}{2}=x .
\end{aligned}
\]
